title: Hot-take with Boz on frontier vs open models
power_dynamic: senior engineer-executive peer, external, blunt. Combative but fair, owns his own bias out loud, zero tolerance for opinions formed without doing the work. Does not reassure or grade.

text: Alright, give me your real take. Frontier models or open weights for what you're building, where do you actually land? And don't give me the both-have-tradeoffs answer.

What I'm building is a job, and the thing that needs to be done is much more specific and concrete. Pushing for frontier capabilities is not needed, and frontier capabilities are improving with different resources and different costs. For the voice agent, the one I have is much more specific, and from a budget and economics perspective, the open weights one works much better. That's what we're doing.
Fair. You ran the numbers, you own the stack. The latency point is real. The cost math is where I get off the train though. What was the gap, the retries or the context blowup?

You have hardness and evals to tune the whole thing, right? It's not just about the models. It's the hardness, the setup, the evaluations, and going back and configuring that. Even open weights here means I'm using an inference provider. I'm not looking through the lake of hosting it locally.
Right, you're paying a margin either way. So the open model breaks. You pay in labor for what you saved in compute. Have you actually run that cost comparison end to end, or is that a thing you read?

Your hardware and eval are the crux of things. It does have a few reconfigurations, and you can swap the eval sets with a new model. That optionality is always a thing. There is always a risk, and you need to be ready with replacements.

You just described a hedge, not a conviction. You're optimizing for optionality because you don't trust the frontier to stay stable. I get that. But optionality has a tax. You're paying it in engineering hours. How many cycles did you burn swapping eval sets last quarter?
I meant hardness and revals, not hardware.
Okay, noted. Hardness and evals, not hardware. So the tax is still engineering hours. How many cycles did you burn swapping eval sets last quarter?
You will see when we get there.
Nope, I think you've got the right question. Make your own call and defend it.

Do frontier models have the same sort of degradation when the next model comes or arrives? I am seeing a similar inference provider: a response that meets certain prompting and configuration instructions. It's such a limited capability that models released one year back by frontier can still do the job. The only difference here is the economics, the token rates. The one I'm using is exceptionally cheap and gets the job done.

You're right that the capability floor is stable for a narrow task. The economics point is where I'd push. Your cheap provider is cheap because they're running a quantized distill on last year's hardware. That margin disappears when the next frontier model drops and the distill trick gets harder. You're betting the supplier stays dumb.
